Enquiry 3: Glyphs, Bark-Paper Books & Zero — Why Were Maya Scribes & Astronomers So Brilliant? (c. AD 300–900)

Big Question: Why do historians celebrate Maya scribes, mathematicians, and astronomers as world pioneers?
Name: _______________________
Date: ________________________
KEY WORDS: Glyphs (Glyphs) Codices (Co-di-ces) Base-20 (Base-twen-ty) El Caracol (El Ca-ra-col) Tzolk'in (Tzol-k'in)
TASK 1 Historical Evidence Detective • Inspect the Clue
Source A: Painted Fig-Bark Page from the Dresden Codex Showing Maya Numbers (c. AD 1200, Copied from Classic Maya Tables)
Zero Clue: Painted on lime-coated fig-bark paper, the Dresden Codex uses a shell symbol for zero—centuries before zero reached Europe!

1a. Inspect Source A. How did the Maya scribe write numbers and sky tables on bark paper?

Starter: "Looking closely at Source A, the Maya scribe painted dots (1), bars (5), and shell zeros on fig-bark paper to..."
TASK 2 Chronology Challenge • Number These Events from 1 (Earliest) to 4 (Latest)
Epigraphers Yuri Knorozov and Tatiana Proskouriakoff unlock phonetic Maya glyphs (AD 1950s–60s)
Maya mathematicians carve the earliest surviving Long Count zero shell inscriptions (c. 36 BC–AD 357)
Spanish Bishop Diego de Landa burns Maya codices—leaving only four surviving bark books (AD 1562)
Maya astronomers paint accurate Venus and eclipse tables inside the Dresden Codex (c. AD 1200)

2b. Quick Explain: Which of these four events mattered most, and why?
